steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper presenting ParlaSent, sentence-level sentiment datasets from parliamentary proceedings in several European languages. Explain why sentiment matters in political discourse, the gap for low-resourced languages and methods, what the datasets are, and summarize the main findings of our experiments.

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Emotions and sentiment in political discourse are considered as crucial and as influential as the substantive policies that elected representatives promote. Since the golden era of research on propaganda, several scholars have shown that emotions play a growing role in affective polarization in politics, and that this has negative consequences for the stability of democratic institutions and for social cohesion. With online media becoming so popular, sentiment analysis has become an indispensable tool to understand the positions of viewers, customers, and voters. It has let all sorts of entrepreneurs know their target audience like never before. Experts on political communication argue that how we receive and process information plays an important role in political decision-making, and that it shapes our judgment with strategic consequences, both for legislators and for the masses. Emotions and sentiment simply play an essential role in political arenas, and politicians have been (ab)using them for decades.

Political scientists generally agree that sentiment analysis is a critical component for understanding political communication in general, but empirical applications outside the English-speaking world are still rare. Also, many research applications in the social sciences lag behind the latest methodological advancements from computational linguistics. This is especially true for studies that analyze political discourse in low-resourced languages, where there are no out-of-the-box tools and this is a huge barrier for social scientists to do this kind of research in the first place. So many applications still rely on dictionary-based methods, which tend to give potentially skewed results, or they approximate sentiment scores based on position-taking stances with relatively high-level generalization (e.g. roll-calls or voting behavior). Field-specific sentiment identifiers trained with machine learning algorithms are comparatively rare. Part of the reason is that training machine learning models can be prohibitively expensive, especially collecting, cleaning, and processing the training data. But recent development in computational linguistics and natural language processing, fueled by transformer-based deep learning models, has lowered the bar for social scientists a lot. This development has also made it possible to adapt existing language models to a specific domain by pre-training the language model additionally on non-annotated domain data.

- The datasets
  - annotated sentence-level datasets, seven European languages: Bosnian, Croatian, Czech, English, Serbian, Slovak, Slovenian
  - parliamentary proceedings of seven countries: Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, Czech Republic, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia, United Kingdom
  - selection: gap in low-resourced languages of Central and Eastern Europe; comparative relevance
  - experiments training sentiment identifiers for political discourse
  - also summary guidelines for social scientists; realistic resource estimates
- Main findings
  - additional pre-training on raw parliamentary data improves performance significantly
  - large 561-million-parameter multilingual models drastically better than half-size ones
  - multilingual models work well on unseen languages
  - multilingual model trained on four times more data from other languages beats language-specific training data on target parliament

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Emotions and sentiment in political discourse are considered as crucial and as influential as the substantive policies that elected representatives promote. Since the golden era of research on propaganda, several scholars have shown that emotions play a growing role in affective polarization in politics, and that this has negative consequences for the stability of democratic institutions and for social cohesion. With online media becoming so popular, sentiment analysis has become an indispensable tool to understand the positions of viewers, customers, and voters. It has let all sorts of entrepreneurs know their target audience like never before. Experts on political communication argue that how we receive and process information plays an important role in political decision-making, and that it shapes our judgment with strategic consequences, both for legislators and for the masses. Emotions and sentiment simply play an essential role in political arenas, and politicians have been (ab)using them for decades.

Political scientists generally agree that sentiment analysis is a critical component for understanding political communication in general, but empirical applications outside the English-speaking world are still rare. Also, many research applications in the social sciences lag behind the latest methodological advancements from computational linguistics. This is especially true for studies that analyze political discourse in low-resourced languages, where there are no out-of-the-box tools and this is a huge barrier for social scientists to do this kind of research in the first place. So many applications still rely on dictionary-based methods, which tend to give potentially skewed results, or they approximate sentiment scores based on position-taking stances with relatively high-level generalization (e.g. roll-calls or voting behavior). Field-specific sentiment identifiers trained with machine learning algorithms are comparatively rare. Part of the reason is that training machine learning models can be prohibitively expensive, especially collecting, cleaning, and processing the training data. But recent development in computational linguistics and natural language processing, fueled by transformer-based deep learning models, has lowered the bar for social scientists a lot. This development has also made it possible to adapt existing language models to a specific domain by pre-training the language model additionally on non-annotated domain data.

In this paper we present annotated sentence-level datasets in seven European languages (Bosnian, Croatian, Czech, English, Serbian, Slovak, and Slovenian), sampled from the parliamentary proceedings of seven European countries (Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, Czech Republic, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia, and United Kingdom). We selected these proceedings because of the existing gap in low-resourced languages of Central and Eastern Europe and because they are relevant in a broader comparative perspective. We use the human-annotated datasets in a series of experiments on training sentiment identifiers that are meant for detecting sentiment in political discourse. Besides its methodological and experimental goals, the paper can also be read as summary guidelines for social scientists who want to train their own sentiment identifiers with a similar scope. We wrote the paper with the intention to make the process of collecting, cleaning, and processing textual data for political science research easier, with realistic estimates of the resources needed. As for the substantial findings, the paper shows that 1) additional pre-training of a language model on raw parliamentary data can significantly improve model performance on sentiment identification; 2) large 561-million-parameter multilingual models perform drastically better than models with half of the parameters; 3) multilingual models also work very well on unseen languages; and 4) even when language-specific training data exist for the parliament proceedings one wants to process, a multilingual model trained on a dataset four times the size from other languages improves the results on the target parliament significantly.

Political scientists generally agree that sentiment analysis is a critical component for understanding political communication in general [1,10,11], but empirical applications outside the English-speaking world are still rare [12,13]. Emotions and sentiment in political discourse are deemed as crucial and influential as the substantive policies promoted by elected representatives [1]. Since the golden era of research on propaganda [2,3], several scholars have demonstrated the growing role of emotions in affective polarization in politics, with negative consequences for the stability of democratic institutions and social cohesion [4,5,6]. With the booming popularity of online media, sentiment analysis has become an indispensable tool for understanding the positions of viewers, customers, and voters [7]. It has allowed all sorts of entrepreneurs to know their target audience like never before [8]. Experts on political communication argue that the way we receive and process information plays an important role in political decision-making, shaping our judgment with strategic consequences both at the level of legislators and of the masses [9]. Emotions and sentiment simply do play an essential role in political arenas, and politicians have been (ab)using them for decades.

Although political scientists generally agree that sentiment analysis represents a critical component for understanding political communication in general [1,10,11], empirical applications outside the English-speaking world are still rare [12,13]. Moreover, many research applications in the social sciences lag behind the latest methodological advancements grounded in computational linguistics. This is especially the case for studies analyzing political discourse in low-resourced languages, where the lack of out-of-the-box tools creates a huge barrier for social scientists to do such research in the first place [14,15,12]. As a result, many applications still rely on dictionary-based methods, which tend to produce potentially skewed results [16,14], or approximate sentiment scores based on position-taking stances with relatively high-level generalization (e.g. roll-calls or voting behavior [17]). Field-specific sentiment identifiers trained using machine learning algorithms are comparatively rare, partly because training machine learning models can be prohibitively expensive, especially when it comes to collecting, cleaning, and processing training data. However, recent developments in computational linguistics and natural language processing, fueled by transformer-based deep learning models, have lowered the bar for social scientists substantially. They have also allowed existing language models to be adapted to a specific domain by additionally pre-training the language model on non-annotated domain data [18].

The paper presents annotated sentence-level datasets in seven European languages (Bosnian, Croatian, Czech, English, Serbian, Slovak, and Slovenian) sampled from the parliamentary proceedings of seven European countries (Bosnia-Herzegovina, Croatia, Czech Republic, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia, and United Kingdom). The human-annotated datasets are used in a series of experiments focused on training sentiment identifiers intended for detecting sentiment in political discourse. Apart from its methodological and experimental goals, the paper can also be read as summary guidelines for social scientists interested in training their own sentiment identifiers with a similar scope. It is written with the intention of facilitating the collection, cleaning, and processing of textual data for political science research, with realistic estimates of the needed resources. In terms of substantial findings, the paper shows that 1) additional pre-training of a language model on raw parliamentary data can significantly improve model performance on the task of sentiment identification; 2) large 561-million-parameter multilingual models perform drastically better than those with half of the parameters; 3) multilingual models also work very well on unseen languages; and finally 4) even when language-specific training data exist for the parliament proceedings one wants to process, a multilingual model trained on a dataset four times the size from other languages improves the results on the target parliament significantly.
